setup: For four thousand years China had been ruled by Chinese — even when foreigners grabbed the north, like the Jurchen Jin who held it for a century, the wealthy, sophisticated Southern Song still governed the rich half from Hangzhou, possibly the largest city on Earth. The Song were the most innovative society alive: paper money, movable type, the compass, gunpowder, the world's most refined bureaucracy. The thing now bearing down on them is the opposite of all that. The Mongols had been chewing through China since 1211; Genghis Khan's grandson Kublai finished the job. In 1271 he proclaimed his own Chinese-style dynasty, the Yuan, and claimed the Mandate of Heaven — the cosmic license to rule that only one dynasty can hold at a time. By claiming it, he was declaring the Song already dead. All that remained was to make it true. What is at stake here is not just a kingdom but a first: all of China, every city and institution, under foreign rule.

bridge: Chapter 1 ended the Song at Yamen in 1279, completing the first conquest of all China by a foreign people. Kublai Khan now holds everything — north and south, some sixty million people, the most refined bureaucracy in the world — but he is a Mongol cavalry leader who cannot read a line of Chinese, sitting on top of a vast Han majority that did not ask for him. Earlier foreign dynasties that grabbed pieces of China, the Khitan and the Jurchen, had all dissolved into Chinese culture within a few generations until they were Chinese in everything but name. Kublai's central problem is how to rule China without that happening to the Mongols.
setup: His answer is to build a whole new kind of state, and this chapter is the machinery of it. He raises a brand-new capital, Khanbaliq — the city we now call Beijing — on a dry northern plain chosen as a compromise between the steppe his power base loved and the China his taxes came from, then extends the thousand-year-old Grand Canal to ship southern rice up to feed it. He stocks the most cosmopolitan court in Asia with Tibetan monks, Persian astronomers, Italian merchants, and Muslim engineers. And he imposes the device meant to keep the conquerors from being absorbed: a four-class legal hierarchy with Mongols on top, Central Asian and Persian "Semu" specialists next, and the Han majority — especially the conquered southerners — at the bottom, locked out of high office. It is a system built to work and to be hated, and both halves of that come true.

bridge: Chapters 1 and 2 showed Kublai Khan finishing the conquest of China and building a state to hold it — a new capital, a rebuilt canal, a court of every religion and tongue in Asia. By the 1270s he is the most powerful single ruler on Earth, and the Mongol war machine that rolled from Korea to the gates of Vienna has nearly run out of places to roll. But Kublai is uneasy. The Mongol nobility suspect he has gone soft and Chinese, and a Mongol Great Khan proves himself by conquering. There is one obvious unconquered prize left, just across the water.
setup: That prize is Japan, ruled since 1185 by a warrior government, the samurai-led bakufu at Kamakura, that simply ignores Kublai's demands for submission. So he builds fleets — and this chapter is about the two catastrophes that follow. In 1274 a force of some 900 ships and 25,000 men lands at Hakata Bay and is hammered, then wrecked by a storm at sea. In 1281 he sends one of the largest amphibious operations the world would see before D-Day — roughly 4,400 ships and 140,000 men — against a Japan that has spent seven years building walls and waiting. Another storm arrives. The Japanese, who had been praying for exactly this, name the wind kamikaze, "divine wind," and fold it into a conviction that the islands are protected by the gods — a belief that runs straight through to the suicide pilots of 1944. What is at stake is the limit of Mongol power, and the founding of a national myth.

bridge: The last three chapters built Kublai Khan's world from the inside — the conquest, the cosmopolitan capital, the failed reach across the sea. This chapter steps outside it, because for one brief window that world was open to the rest of the planet. The Mongol Empire had fractured into four khanates, but they still shared a postal network, trade passports, and family ties stretching from Korea to Hungary. For about sixty years a merchant in Italy and a friar in Beijing were genuinely, if barely, connected. This is the era of that connection, and the most famous person who traveled it.
setup: In 1275 a twenty-one-year-old Venetian named Marco Polo reaches Kublai's court and stays seventeen years; the book he later dictates from a Genoese prison becomes the most influential travel account ever written and, two centuries on, the thing Columbus thought he was sailing toward. But this chapter handles Polo carefully, because scholars have argued for two hundred years over how much of him is real — the gaps in his story, the romance-writer who shaped his prose, the claims no Chinese record confirms. And he was not alone: a Christian monk born in Beijing, Rabban Sauma, traveled the other way to meet the Pope and the kings of France and England, and a friar named John of Montecorvino became the first Catholic archbishop of Beijing. The real subject is the two-way Eurasian exchange the Mongols made possible — and why the West remembers only its half of it.

bridge: Chapter 2 noted, almost in passing, one of the four-class system's sharpest edges: Kublai suspended the civil-service examinations in 1271 and they stayed gone for forty-four years. That sounds like an administrative footnote. It was not. The examinations were the entire reason for being of China's educated class — the Han literati had organized their families, identities, and careers around passing them for centuries. Pulling the exams away cut tens of thousands of trained, ambitious, suddenly purposeless men loose. This chapter is about what they did with that freedom.
setup: What they did was invent, or perfect, most of the Chinese popular culture that still exists. Locked out of government, the displaced literati poured their training into things the state did not control: vernacular drama written in everyday speech instead of stiff classical Chinese; the earliest stable versions of the great novels Romance of the Three Kingdoms and Water Margin; ink landscape painting; a calligraphy revival. The playwright Guan Hanqing wrote tragedies still performed today; the Four Yuan Masters painted scrolls that defined "Chinese landscape" forever after. The deep irony is the whole point of the chapter: the dynasty's most discriminatory policy produced its most enduring gift. A foreign regime that shut Han scholars out of office accidentally handed Chinese civilization its popular literary tradition.

bridge: Chapter 4 sketched the open roads of the Pax Mongolica — the postal relays and trade passports that let Marco Polo and Rabban Sauma cross half the world. This chapter follows what actually moved along them. With the Mongol khanates keeping the peace from China to the Mediterranean, the Yuan ran what was probably the largest integrated commercial economy the pre-modern world had ever seen: silk and porcelain west, Persian cobalt and astronomy east, all of it humming through one connected network. It was a golden age of trade. It was also, it turned out, a delivery system.
setup: The chapter has two faces. The bright one is the commerce: the port of Quanzhou, which Marco Polo and the Moroccan traveler Ibn Battuta both describe as the busiest harbor on Earth, packed with Arab, Persian, Tamil, and Christian merchants; the Yuan paper money that astonished Europeans who had never seen currency backed by nothing but a government's word; the blue-and-white porcelain, born here for the Islamic export market, that still says "China" to the world. The dark face is the bacterium. The same caravan routes that carried silk west almost certainly carried Yersinia pestis out of Inner Asia — and in 1346, through the besieged Crimean port of Kaffa and onto fleeing Genoese ships, it reached Europe as the Black Death, killing perhaps a third of the continent. The very integration that made the network rich is what made it lethal. Casualty figures and the exact disease trail are debated; the connection is not.

bridge: Chapter 2 built Kublai's brilliant, contradiction-riddled machine; Chapters 5 and 6 showed its culture flowering and its trade booming. But Kublai died in 1294, and the genius did not pass down with the throne. This chapter is the long unraveling. The Mongols had never developed a stable rule for who inherits, and Kublai had locked his princes away in the palace to keep them harmless — which mostly made them weak, dependent on the eunuchs and dowagers who raised them. After one steady successor, the whole thing came apart.
setup: The numbers tell it: in the thirty-nine years after 1307 the throne changed hands nine times, four emperors were assassinated, and at one point two emperors and a regent were murdered inside nine months. Onto that political wreckage the chapter piles three more disasters, all reinforcing each other. The paper money that once amazed Marco Polo (Chapter 6) was over-printed into worthless confetti, wiping out tax revenue and ruining peasants. The Yellow River — "China's Sorrow" — burst its banks in 1344, and the brutal forced-labor project to fix it created exactly the army of furious, brutalized conscripts that would rise against the dynasty. And a Buddhist apocalyptic movement, the White Lotus, told the desperate that the future Buddha was coming to sweep the corrupt foreign rulers away. In 1351 peasants tied red cloths around their heads and the Red Turban rebellions exploded. What is at stake is whether a dynasty can survive every kind of crisis at once. It cannot.

bridge: Chapter 7 left the Yuan in pieces: a paralyzed court, a worthless currency, the Yellow River disaster, and the Red Turban rebellions tearing across central China after 1351. The dynasty that Kublai built was effectively finished; what remained was to see who would inherit the wreckage. Out of the religious networks and the famine-struck villages of the Red Turban world, one man would climb further than anyone in Chinese history — from an orphaned beggar to the founder of the dynasty that replaced the Mongols.
setup: This chapter is the rise of Zhu Yuanzhang. Born to illiterate peasants in 1328, orphaned by the post-flood famine at sixteen, he survived as a begging Buddhist monk, joined a Red Turban band at twenty-four, and turned out to be one of the great military minds of the age. He out-fought every rival warlord — most decisively at the colossal naval battle of Lake Poyang in 1363 — took Nanjing, and in 1368 proclaimed himself the Hongwu Emperor of the Ming, "bright" rule replacing the dark Yuan. His armies pushed north and the last Mongol emperor fled Beijing into the steppe without a fight. But the chapter's real weight is the reckoning: what the foreign dynasty actually left behind — Beijing as the capital, Tibetan Buddhism, the vernacular novels, a vastly larger conception of China's territory — and the argument, still unsettled today, over whether the Yuan was a Chinese dynasty ruled by Mongols or a Mongol occupation that only looked Chinese.
